title: Garfield County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Garfield County wells have a median depth of 102 feet. See local yields, water levels, drilling costs and checks to make before buying land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Garfield County
intro_html:
A well near Rifle is not a reliable price guide for a lot outside Carbondale. Garfield County covers mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, and the countywide median depth of 102 feet is a starting point—not a drilling specification.

Colorado DWR records contain 12,083 permitted wells in the county, with 5,978 recorded as constructed. Use the depth, yield and cost figures below to frame your budget, then narrow the search to neighboring wells around Silt, New Castle, Glenwood Springs or the area where you plan to buy.

sections.heading: A 102-Foot Median Leaves Plenty of Room in the Bid
sections.html:
Among 7,198 wells reporting depth, the median is 102 feet, and the middle half runs from 53 to 190 feet. That range matters more to a buyer than the median alone: nearby records toward the deeper end call for a different drilling allowance than shallow neighboring completions. The 90th-percentile depth is 290 feet.

Ground conditions help explain the spread. Permits identify 135 Alluvial wells and 84 Williams Fork wells, while 11,611 fall under unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. That broad label does not establish the formation beneath your parcel. Around Cattle Creek, Parachute or Battlement Mesa, compare nearby completion logs and terrain before asking a driller to commit to a depth estimate.

sections.heading: Garfield County Yield Reports Favor Useful Flow
sections.html:
The 2,234 reported pump yields have a median of 15.0 gpm, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. Those reported rates are encouraging for household planning, but a permit-record yield is not a guarantee of sustained flow during daily use.

Low production still deserves attention: 1% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, and 9% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. A buyer looking at a low-yield well should ask about recovery, storage and pump controls rather than simply accepting that water comes from the tap. Request a current pumping and recovery test, and keep physical production separate from the uses legally allowed by the permit.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth to standing water before pumping, not the bottom of the well. Garfield County's 868 reported measurements have a median of 38 feet below ground; the middle half is 19–75 feet. A shallow standing level does not mean the well can be drilled only that deep.

The decade medians fluctuate: 30 feet in the 1960s, 53 in the 1980s, 30 in the 2000s and 39 in the 2020s. This series does not establish a steadily dropping water table. These are countywide groups of measurements, not repeated readings from an unchanged set of wells. For a particular property, seek dated measurements and compare static level, pumping level and recovery.

sections.heading: The Permit Record Is Busiest in the 1990s
sections.html:
Garfield County issued 2,951 permits in the 1990s, followed by 2,500 in the 2000s and 1,543 in the 2010s. The 2020s account for 852 permits, with the newest permit year listed as 2026. The current decade is incomplete, so its total is not directly comparable with a finished decade.

Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) leads the listed driller records with 3,432 entries. Collins Drilling Co (Collins, F. E. "Bodie") has 730. Another 852 appear under the label Authorized (Pe, Pg); treat that as a record label rather than a contractor recommendation. Domestic/household use accounts for 58% of records and monitoring for 25%, so not every mapped permit represents a residential supply well.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole in Garfield County
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $50–$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 102-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $5,100–$7,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $11,100–$19,600.

Those figures are a budgeting baseline, not a parcel quote. A lot near El Jebel with straightforward access may present different construction demands than a constrained site outside No Name. Ask the bid to spell out casing, grout, development, testing and the connection to the house. Confirm what is included, what is billed by actual depth and what happens to the price if the planned completion does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Failed-Well Risk Separately
sections.html:
The mapped environmental screen lists 691 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 74 historic mine features and 13 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These are screening flags—not proof that a particular Garfield County well is contaminated. A sampling location also does not, by itself, establish a detection.

Review nearby site records and arrange laboratory testing suited to the property's surroundings and intended drinking-water use. A yield test cannot establish water quality. Likewise, reported successful yields do not guarantee that a new bore will produce. Ask about nearby unsuccessful drilling, and settle the contract terms for an unproductive hole. Check wellhead condition, casing and grout records, and proposed septic placement before fixing the house footprint.

sections.heading: Before Buying in Silt, Rifle or Carbondale
sections.html:
Start with the actual parcel, not the county average. Pull its DWR permit, completion report and available test records, then compare neighboring wells in similar ground. A nearby well across a change in terrain may be a poor guide even when it looks close on the map.

Confirm that the permit authorizes your intended household, livestock or outdoor use; a productive well does not automatically authorize every use. New permits depend on location and water-law constraints, and augmentation may be required in over-appropriated basins. Before closing or designing a build, coordinate the well location with septic approval, equipment access, utility trenching and the house site. Make unresolved water supply and permit questions part of your purchase due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Garfield County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 102 feet, and the middle half of wells runs from 53 to 190 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 290 feet. These figures come from 7,198 depth reports across the county. For a drilling estimate, nearby completion logs in similar ground are more useful than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Garfield County?
faq.a: The cost model uses $50–$75 per foot. At the median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,100–$7,600, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $11,100–$19,600. Ask for a parcel-specific bid that identifies casing, grout, access requirements and charges if drilling must continue deeper.

faq.q: How much water do Garfield County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a median of 15.0 gpm, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. Of the reported yields, 1% are under 1 gpm and 9% are in the 1–5 gpm band. Have an existing well tested for sustained output and recovery rather than relying solely on an old reported yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Garfield County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through testing. The local environmental screen includes 691 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 74 historic mine features and 13 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped locations do not prove contamination at your property. Review nearby records and choose laboratory testing appropriate to the site's potential exposures.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Garfield County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady countywide decline. Median depth to water was 53 feet in the 1980s, 30 feet in the 2000s and 39 feet in the 2020s. These groups are not a same-well monitoring series. Evaluate dated water levels and pumping performance at the property before drawing a local conclusion.
